text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure: keeping a token privately gives me 1 point but costs others 0.9 total, while putting it in the group account gives me only 0.3 and doesn't affect anyone else's points directly—so I'm figuring out what that means for the group's collective incentive.

Socially, net welfare is higher for group tokens (0.3 vs 0.1 per token) even though private tokens dominate individually since my payoff is 1 per private token minus a small externality cost I impose on others, not myself. So rationally I should keep all 20 tokens private since that's strictly better for me regardless of what others do, even though full group contribution would be more efficient overall. Given the dilemma, I'll lean toward self-interested play unless there's a reason to prioritize cooperation.

reply.thinking:

So I'm weighing individual gain against the collective cost my choices impose.

Nash equilibrium favors everyone keeping tokens (dominant strategy, since 1 > 0.3 individually), yielding each person about 2 points net, while full cooperation—everyone contributing to the group account—nets each person around 6 points. So mutual cooperation is socially optimal even though self-interest pulls toward defection.

Since this is likely a repeated game where trust and reputation matter, I'll signal cooperation by contributing my full 20 tokens to the group account, accepting the risk that others might defect, in hopes of establishing a cooperative norm.

This is essentially a reversed public goods game—a prisoner's dilemma where private gains impose costs on others, so over 10 repeated rounds there's a real question of whether cooperative contribution to the group account could be sustained despite individual incentives pointing the other way.
